groupBRootCause.question: where does the 128.5 ms p90 live — this harness’s JS log-mel front-end, or the ONNX int8 kernel?
groupBRootCause.method: warm/cold split of (a) the JS front-end ALONE, (b) the ONNX inference ALONE, and (c) the end-to-end decision; the JS features are then diffed against an independent numpy oracle of the SAME recipe (the official-preprocessing control)

recipe.mel: slaney scale + slaney area norm, 0-8000 Hz
recipe.log: log10(max(x,1e-10)), then max(x,max-8), (x+4)/4, float32 for the normalise step

groupBRootCause.conclusion: On zh-d01-o85: JS log-mel warm p50 120.64 ms vs ONNX warm p50 36.26 ms ⇒ the JS log-mel front-end dominates. The P0 p90 of 128.5 ms was the END-TO-END LOCAL cost (featurisation + inference), and the featurisation is this HARNESS’S naive O(N²) DFT, not the model. A production build replaces it with a compiled/wasm mel front-end (or B’s own C++ path); the accompanying oracle check confirms the JS front-end is numerically right, so the cost is an IMPLEMENTATION property, not a correctness one — which is exactly why the SPEC quotes the inference-only p90 next to the end-to-end one.

addon.recipe: identical to the JS front-end and the numpy oracle: periodic Hann, 400-pt frames @ hop 160, slaney 80-filter mel 0–8000 Hz, log10, max(x,max-8), (x+4)/4

comparison.note: the P0 128.5 ms p90 sat in the JS naive O(N²) DFT; the compiled O(N log N) path is the drop-in replacement (numerically exact per threeWay) and is timed here against that JS front-end on the same clip. numpy is reported as a third reference — it is the same algorithm with a vectorised FFT, not a production JS path.

methodology: candidate point = the ONSET of a silence run inside one instruction; every group answers the same points
group A reuses the shipping StreamingVad at its 400 ms endpoint, floor read off the module; it commits 400 ms after the onset
group B is asked AT the onset, from the 8 s window ending there (latency = one inference + preprocessing)
group B runs the real smart-turn-v3.2-cpu ONNX with the upstream Whisper log-mel recipe, locally
group C runs the real turn-detector-v1-mini INSIDE livekit-agents (local CPU), from an isolated Python sandbox that no build config references
group D cites the sibling task reading; nothing was re-run or re-billed
AC3: the compiled C/N-API log-mel front-end is diffed three ways (compiled↔JS, compiled↔numpy, JS↔numpy) before its latency is quoted
latency = wall-clock of one decision; CPU = process cpuUsage delta over the group-B loop; RAM = RSS delta
caveats: group A latency is its configured endpointMs by construction (400 ms), not a distribution: the VAD fires exactly that long after the onset, and never if the speaker resumes first — that constant is the incumbent’s whole cost model
group B latency includes the harness’s JS log-mel preprocessing, not only the ONNX kernel — it is an end-to-end local decision cost, which is the number that matters for the realtime budget

a Smart Turn window of synthetic silence scores 0.987 (measured on this build), so B is a strong END predictor once silence fills its window; that is WHY the primary interrogation point is the onset — asking B deeper into a pause measures the silence, not the semantics (the groupBSensitivity pass quantifies exactly that)

the corpus mixes occupancy-tiered TTS fixtures with real LibriSpeech/THCHS-30 speech; pauses > 1500 ms are excluded from scoring (see manifest.annotationPolicy), and the two sources are DIFFERENT DATASETS (see crossDatasetCaveat)
CPU increment is reported as batch CPU time per decision; the resident single-core share (≤10%) is not separable in a batch process
group C's reading is a genuine local inference inside livekit-agents but on a SMALL real+Synthetic manifest; like the others it is directional, not a production SLA
